items.item: Padding bytes are not guaranteed to be zero, and nothing in the language initializes them on a stack allocation; a program that happens to see zeros there in testing can see something else entirely under a different allocator, a different build, or after the same memory is reused

at.step: The same padding that cost bytes now costs soundness

items.item: bytemuck's Pod derive check is a real, mechanical analysis of the type's declared layout (size, alignment, and field offsets, the same facts topic 16's offset_of! computed), not a heuristic or a lint that can be silenced; there is no way to derive Pod on a type with padding short of removing the padding itself

NoUninit and Pod are deliberately not the same trait: NoUninit only rules out padding, while Pod (via Zeroable) also requires that any all-zero bit pattern be a valid value of the type, which is a stronger and separate property from having no padding at all

bytemuck::from_bytes is not unconditionally safe to call with any byte slice; it still panics at run time if the slice's length or alignment doesn't match the target type, which is a real, checked runtime condition, distinct from the compile-time padding check the derive performs on the type itself

at.step: A padding-free header, read with no unsafe code at all

items.item: A hand-rolled transmute or pointer-cast reinterpret of the same padded byte buffer would compile without complaint and might even produce plausible-looking output most of the time, which is exactly what makes this bug class dangerous: the failure is undefined behaviour, not a guaranteed crash, so it can pass every test that happens not to expose it

Endianness and padding are two independent problems that both happen to live in this topic because both concern reading someone else's bytes: a type can have zero padding and still be read wrong if its multi-byte fields' byte order doesn't match the sender's, and fixing one of the two problems does nothing for the other

at.step: Big-endian, little-endian, and the one wrong default

items.item: This topic's own sandbox is little-endian (x86_64), which is why to_ne_bytes happens to agree with to_le_bytes here; the reel's claim is not that native order is always wrong, only that it is never guaranteed to match a wire format's chosen order, which is why portable code must never use to_ne_bytes/from_ne_bytes for data that crosses a boundary

items.item: Choosing bytemuck over zerocopy for this chapter is a scope decision, not a claim that one crate is strictly better; zerocopy's FromBytes/IntoBytes traits solve the same padding problem with a different, more finely split trait hierarchy, named in the Deep dive rather than built here to keep one running example

Every number and every compiler diagnostic in this topic's reel is copied from a real execution of examples.py on this sandbox's toolchain (rustc 1.97.0, bytemuck resolved via cargo from crates.io), not invented or quoted from the crate's own documentation examples
